newsitem.title: ALBANIA: More anti-government protests in Albania's south.
newsitem.headline: More anti-government protests in Albania's south.

text.p: Anti-government protests in Albania's south showed no sign of abating on Sunday as about 5,000 marchers staged their 18th daily protest march along the palm-lined main boulevard of this Adriatic port town.

The Balkan country's relatively more prosperous south has been hardest hit by the collapse of five dubious pyramid investment schemes last month which wiped out the life savings of hundreds of thousands of Albanians.

Destitute investors blame the right-wing government of President Sali Berisha and Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi for not clamping down on the schemes when they boomed and keeping hapless investors in the dark about their dangers.
"We are demonstrating both because we want our money back and we want the government to resign," protester Engjell Dine said. "We're determined to keep on going until the bitter end."
The demonstrators rallied in front of Vlore university to express their support for a group of 55 students who went on an anti-government hunger strike on Thursday.

"The main purpose of our hunger strike is to force the government to resign as soon as possible and for a technical government to be formed to deal with the problems which are hurting our city," student leader Leonhard Kagtalli told Reuters.
Berisha last week embarked on a election campaign-style tour across Albania to tell his desperate people that only the ruling Democratic Party could resolve the crisis.

But his office on Sunday said Berisha had no immediate plans to travel to the country's south, which has spearheaded opposition against his government since five fraudulent funds collapsed in January, sparking weeks of popular protest.
Sources close to the presidency had indicated on Saturday that Berisha was due to travel to the town of Fiere, some 110 km (70 miles) south of Tirana, on Sunday.

Adressing hand-picked supporters in several cities across central and northern Albania over the past week, Berisha has promised to step up economic growth and exempt some of the worst-hit investors from paying taxes for two years.
The opposition has said it will not rest until Berisha and his government resign, but not before reimbursing Albanians for the hundreds of thousands of dollars they have lost.

In an interview with Reuters late on Saturday, Democratic Party chairman and Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu defended the government's record. He said there was no question of Meksi's resignation at the moment but added that the final decision would be up to the party leadership.

"For the moment, this is not the case. We'll be discussing everything in some time in the national council of the party, but for the moment we're only thinking about having contact with our people," Shehu said.

Mirroring similar remarks by Berisha on Saturday, blamed the opposition Socialists for exploiting the country's crisis to regain power: "I don't think there's an anti-government feeling in the country. It is the opposition that has used this situation."
The key opposition Socialists changed their name from the Communist Party after Albania emerged from 45 years of ruthless Stalinist isolation in 1990.

"The communists thought it was the right time to swallow Albanian democracy but we will never allow them to take power again," Berisha told a boisterous crowd of 4,000 supporters in the northern town of Shkoder on Saturday.
